newsitem.title: USA: Simpson II - how will it play with no TV?.
newsitem.headline: Simpson II - how will it play with no TV?.

text.p: What if they held an O.J. Simpson trial and nobody watched?

When Simpson's civil trial begins on Tuesday, it will be under heavy scrutiny from legal experts looking to gauge how justice is served without the ever-present courtroom TV camera that made his criminal trial one of the most sensational U.S. court cases ever and a huge television event.

O.J. Simpson's criminal trial attracted worldwide attention in part because the courtroom drama, climaxing in the ex-football star's acquittal last October on double-murder charges that he killed his wife and a man, was played out on live television.
Proponents of cameras in the courtroom saw the yearlong trial as endorsing their argument that in a democratic system, the citizenry should see justice in action.
But opponents say the Simpson trial degenerated into a media circus and was an example of the worst kind of excess television can fuel.

Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki, the no-nonsense jurist who is presiding over Simpson's civil trial, clearly differed with Judge Lance Ito, who was in charge of the first trial and was accused by many analysts of losing control of his courtroom.

Ito's decision to allow every twist and turn of the trial to be televised, guaranteed the case would become a ratings success on U.S. television, bumping regular afternoon soap-operas off the air for what many called a real-life drama.
It also made celebrities of many of the previously unknown lawyers and witnesses who suddenly found themselves thrust into the glare of international publicity.

Without the cameras, this public display of the U.S. justice system in action would never have merited headlines from Africa to Australia or daily half-hour trial highlights on British TV, especially for a case involving a sports star and bit-part actor who was originally all but unknown outside North America.
It may not be repeated, since Fujisaki barred cameras and audio recorders from his courtroom, as well as issuing a gag order preventing lawyers and witnesses from talking about the case in public.

Experts were divided on what effect the absence of cameras will have on the second Simpson trial, in which he faces wrongful death lawsuits filed by the families of the murder victims, his ex-wife Nicole Brown and her friend Ronald Goldman.
UCLA law professor Peter Arenella likened the case to that of the Menendez brothers, who were convicted this year of murdering their wealthy Beverly Hills parents at a second, untelevised trial.

Their first trial, under the glare of TV cameras in court, attracted big headlines and ended in deadlocked juries. "Menendez II had the same plot lines (as Simpson), but because there were no cameras in court, the case did not achieve the same amount of media attention," said Arenella.

"The justification for televising the first trial was to show that Simpson got a fair trial," he said. "(But) by televising the trial, most Americans mistakenly thought that they were seeing it from the same point of view as the jury, so they felt they could make their own judgment too.
"But TV did not show what the jury saw, like the bloody pictures. Also viewers could hear all the other stuff from TV commentators and pundits, so it all gets mixed up," Arenella argued.
He said that with less TV coverage of Simpson's civil trial, Americans -- most of whom get the majority of their news from television -- would not learn as much about the case.
But Arenella said he remained opposed to courtroom cameras in high-profile like Simpson's because such cases "generate media attention that equals media frenzy."
Despite the ban on cameras and tape recorders in the Santa Monica court for Simpson II, the nationwide cable station Court TV plans extensive coverage.

"We'd be insane not to give it attention, despite what we hear about people being burned out on the case. We've had lots of calls and Internet requests for coverage," said Eric Sorensen, executive producer of Court TV.
Unlike the first trial when it covered every moment inside the courtroom, this time Court TV's coverage will include reports at every break along with a heavy dose of analysis.
The legal community remains divided over the issue of televising trials.

Many judges blamed cameras for the spectacle in Simpson's first trial, and legal experts say this will cause a backlash in state courts and kill any chance of lifting the ban on TV cameras in federal trials for years to come.
